source.title: Training compute-optimal transformer encoder models
source.authors: Megi Dervishi; Alexandre Allauzen; Gabriel Synnaeve; Yann LeCun

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures training-loss scaling and compute-optimal allocation using scaling-law sweeps, fitting, and extrapolation, applying these measurements to encoder MLM models rather than decoder NTP models.
record.gate_note: Results from cited prior studies and baseline scores retrieved from other papers are not recorded as this study's results. Downstream MTEB scores follow supervised contrastive fine-tuning; the paper explicitly notes that this makes it difficult to isolate pretraining alone.
record.test_reason: The study applies the original methods (isoFLOP parabolas, Chinchilla parametric loss fit, compute-optimal allocation, extrapolation to a larger run) in a new setting: bidirectional encoders trained with MLM on Fineweb_edu. Its own runs bear on V1, V2, V3, V6 and V7. It is T3 rather than T1 because the model class and objective differ from the originals, and compute uses FN, which counts attention FLOPs, rather than 6N.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Additions: the authors put the compute-optimal encoder data-to-model ratio at about 10–100, versus about 3 for decoders. They say decoder laws do not transfer to encoders, and this does not follow from the masking ratio (effective-data rescaling rejected). OptiBERT matches or surpasses NeoBERT and ModernBERT on MTEB with 50–1000× less compute.
record.recipe_differences: Uses scaling-law sweeps, compute-optimal allocation fitting, and parametric loss modeling associated with decoder studies, but tests bidirectional encoder transformers trained with MLM rather than decoder-only NTP. Compute uses FN to account for attention FLOPS; training loss is used as a validation-loss estimator on the stated infinite-data regime.
record.method_sensitivity: Allocation exponents vary numerically between parabolic and parametric fitting (r4–r9), although the authors describe the approaches as equivalent and the reported uncertainties overlap. The paper also states that the dataset, optimizer, scheduler, tokenizer, and architecture can affect results but holds most of these fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal learning rate and batch size follow power laws in compute (lr ∼ 69·C^-0.24, bs ∼ 17.38·C^0.24), with large variance and a broad optimal region.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal optimizer hyperparameters scale as power laws in compute for MLM encoders.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher masking ratios are favoured at larger compute, and the masking ratio shows no relation to the optimal data-to-model ratio (Fig. 6, MTEB v2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLM data hunger is not explained by the effective-token rescaling D' = M·D.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: All scaling experiments use one fixed English dataset, Fineweb_edu, and hold many factors fixed; the paper notes limited coverage of optimizer, scheduler, tokenizer, and architecture choices. Downstream evaluation is limited and requires fine-tuning; the authors also caution that the simple fine-tuning data may be restrictive for models larger than 1B parameters.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 reports task-specific GLUE scores for each model; these task-level values are omitted to retain the aggregate GLUE measure relevant to downstream predictability. Individual MTEB task-category scores are also omitted; the paper reports the MTEB aggregate scores in r12–r23 and discusses weaker Clustering, Retrieval, and Reranking performance in the accompanying text.

untested.parts: Held-out validation loss (training loss is used instead), other datasets, and decoder or other model classes.
Extrapolation to more than one larger run, or beyond roughly 2 orders of magnitude past the fitted range.
Allocation under other datasets, schedules, tokenizers, or parameter counting by N rather than FN.
Not tested: width-to-depth is fixed near 64, and the authors note sensitivity is possible.
Not tested: no other modalities, repeated-data regime, or power-law fit for fine-tuning or transfer.
Downstream performance without fine-tuning, a fitted functional form for downstream versus compute or loss, and models above 1B parameters.
Curvature away from a single power law, and dependence on dataset, schedule or optimizer; all are held fixed.

missing.what: OptiBERTneo MTEB(eng,v2) averages of 47.4, 50.5 and 52.6 at 1.3B, 13B and 130B tokens
MTEB(eng,v1) averages for all 8 compute-optimal OptiBERT models; plotted only, values not stated
Extrapolated parametric loss contour and compute-optimal path to C = 3e21

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Model size is measured as FN (FLOPs per token, including attention), so exponents are not directly comparable to N-based laws. The record's V6 label on MTEB task categories versus SOTA was dropped: it compares against other models and is not a scaling result. Per-category MTEB v2 scores (declared left out) are non-monotonic for Clustering and Reranking, a possible further V6 limit. The GLUE 'non-monotonic' claim in the record is incorrect.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses training loss as an estimator of validation loss and tests encoder-only MLM models on one English dataset; it does not establish the relationship for all language models or data regimes.
Tests one reported high-compute run; it does not test extrapolation across multiple larger model families or other settings.

The fitted allocation laws are for encoder MLM models and the study's compute definition and tested range; it does not establish the allocation for other architectures, objectives, datasets, or schedules.
Architecture width, depth, and other design choices are not systematically varied to measure their effect on loss.
No other modalities, repeated-data regime, or power-law tests of fine-tuning or transfer are conducted.
Downstream scaling is evaluated on MTEB and GLUE after fine-tuning; the study does not establish general downstream predictability across tasks or without fine-tuning.

The study reports encoder-versus-decoder differences and two fitting approaches, but does not systematically vary data, schedule, parameter-counting conventions, or fitting choices to establish their individual effects. It does not report curves bending away from a single power law.
